slides.title: What is a Fraction?
slides.subtitle: A fraction represents part of a whole divided into equal pieces.
slides.keyConcept: Top = Numerator (how many pieces you have), Bottom = Denominator (total pieces the whole is cut into).
points: 1/2 means 1 piece out of 2 equal halves.
The bottom number (Denominator) MUST never be zero!
If you eat 3 slices of an 8-slice pizza, you ate 3/8 of the pizza.

example.problem: You slice a cake into 4 equal slices and eat 1 slice. What fraction did you eat?
example.note: 1 slice eaten (numerator) out of 4 total slices (denominator).

slides.title: Visualizing Fractions
slides.subtitle: See how pieces form a complete unit.
slides.keyConcept: The larger the denominator, the smaller each individual slice is!
points: 1/2 is much bigger than 1/8 because 2 big slices beat 8 tiny slivers.
When numerator = denominator (e.g. 4/4 or 5/5), the fraction equals 1 whole.
Proper fractions have numerator < denominator (e.g., 2/3, 5/8).

example.problem: Which is larger: 1/3 or 1/5 of the same candy bar?
example.note: Dividing into 3 parts makes bigger pieces than dividing into 5 parts.

slides.title: Equivalent Fractions
slides.subtitle: Different numbers, exactly the same value!
slides.keyConcept: Multiply or divide top and bottom by the SAME number to find equivalent fractions.
points: 1/2 is identical in amount to 2/4, 3/6, and 4/8.
Simplifying: divide numerator and denominator by their greatest common factor.
4/8 simplifies to 1/2 by dividing both top & bottom by 4.

example.problem: What is 2/6 simplified to its simplest form?

slides.title: Adding Like Fractions
slides.subtitle: When denominators match, simply add the tops!
slides.keyConcept: Keep the bottom number unchanged! Only add the top numbers.
points: Never add denominators! 1/4 + 1/4 is 2/4 (which is 1/2), NOT 2/8.
Check if your final answer can be simplified.

example.problem: Calculate 2/7 + 3/7

slides.title: What is Direct Proportion?
slides.subtitle: When one quantity increases, the other increases at the exact same rate!
slides.keyConcept: Direct relationship: Double one, the other doubles. Triple one, the other triples!
points: Formula: y = k · x, where k is the constant ratio (k = y / x).
If 1 notebook costs $3, then 2 notebooks cost $6, 3 cost $9.
The ratio (Cost ÷ Notebooks) is always constant: $3.

example.problem: If 1 ice cream costs $2.50, how much do 4 ice creams cost?
example.note: 4 × $2.50 = $10.00. Both quantity and cost scaled by 4.

slides.title: The Constant of Proportionality (k)
slides.subtitle: The secret multiplier connecting two variables.
slides.keyConcept: Find k = y ÷ x first. Once you know k, you can solve for any unknown value!
points: Example: A car drives 120 km in 2 hours.
k = 120 ÷ 2 = 60 km per hour (unit rate).
In 5 hours, the car travels: 5 × 60 = 300 km.

example.problem: A machine packs 90 boxes in 3 minutes. Find the unit rate (k).

slides.title: The Cross-Multiplication Method
slides.subtitle: Solve any proportion ratio with this quick shortcut.
slides.keyConcept: If a/b = c/d, then a × d = b × c.
points: Set up the proportion: (items₁) / (cost₁) = (items₂) / (cost₂).
Cross multiply diagonally, then divide by the remaining number.
Works for recipes, currency conversion, scale models, and fuel mileage.

example.problem: If 3 pencils cost $1.50, how much do 7 pencils cost?

slides.title: Direct Proportion in Daily Life
slides.subtitle: From kitchens to road trips, direct proportion is everywhere.
slides.keyConcept: Always check: Does zero input equal zero output? Does doubling input double output?
points: Cooking recipes: Doubling guests means doubling flour, eggs, and sugar.
Salary per hour: Work twice the hours, earn twice the wage.
Graph of direct proportion is ALWAYS a straight line passing through the origin (0,0).

example.problem: A recipe for 4 pancakes needs 1 cup milk. How much milk for 12 pancakes?

slides.title: What is Indirect Proportion?
slides.subtitle: When one quantity increases, the other DECREASES proportionally!
slides.keyConcept: Inverse relationship: As one variable doubles (×2), the other cuts in half (÷2)!
points: Example: More workers on a project means FEWER days needed to finish.
Driving faster (higher speed) means LESS time to reach destination.
Unlike direct proportion, they move in OPPOSITE directions.

example.problem: If 2 painters take 6 hours to paint a room, how long will 4 painters take?
example.note: Painters doubled (×2), so time required is cut in half (÷2): 6 ÷ 2 = 3 hours.

slides.title: The Constant Product Rule
slides.subtitle: The master formula for all inverse proportion problems.
slides.keyConcept: In indirect proportion, the PRODUCT of the two variables is always CONSTANT: x · y = k.
points: x₁ · y₁ = x₂ · y₂ = k
Example: 2 workers × 6 days = 12 worker-days (total work k).
For 3 workers: 3 × days = 12  →  days = 12 ÷ 3 = 4 days!

example.problem: 4 taps fill a tank in 30 minutes. How long for 2 taps?

slides.title: Speed vs. Travel Time
slides.subtitle: The classic real-world inverse proportion.
slides.keyConcept: Distance = Speed × Time. When distance is fixed, Speed and Time are inversely proportional.
points: Traveling at 60 km/h takes 2 hours (60 × 2 = 120 km total).
If you speed up to 120 km/h: time = 120 ÷ 120 = 1 hour.
If you slow down to 30 km/h: time = 120 ÷ 30 = 4 hours.

example.problem: At 50 km/h, a trip takes 4 hours. How long at 100 km/h?
example.note: Total distance = 50 × 4 = 200 km. At 100 km/h: 200 / 100 = 2 hours.

slides.title: Spotting Direct vs. Indirect
slides.subtitle: Never confuse direct and indirect proportions again!
slides.keyConcept: Ask yourself: Does more of A mean MORE of B (Direct) or LESS of B (Indirect)?
points: Direct (y/x = k): More apples = higher cost. More fuel = further distance.
Indirect (x · y = k): More people sharing food = smaller share per person.
Indirect graph is a downward curved hyperbola, never a straight line.

example.problem: A box of 24 chocolates is shared equally among friends. Direct or indirect?
example.note: More friends = fewer chocolates per friend! (Friends × Chocolates = 24).

slides.title: What is a Percentage?
slides.subtitle: Percent literally means 'per one hundred' (out of 100).
slides.keyConcept: Symbol % = / 100. Any percentage is just a fraction with 100 as its denominator!
points: 50% means 50 out of 100 (which is 1/2).
100% means the entire whole (100/100 = 1).
7% means 7 out of every 100.

example.problem: In a box of 100 marbles, 35 are green. What percentage is green?

slides.title: The Super Benchmark %
slides.subtitle: Mental math shortcuts to calculate percentages in your head instantly.
slides.keyConcept: Memorize these 4 benchmarks: 50% = half, 25% = quarter, 10% = divide by 10, 1% = divide by 100.
points: To find 10% of any number: just move the decimal point 1 spot left! (10% of 70 = 7).
To find 50%: divide by 2 (50% of 84 = 42).
To find 20%: find 10% and double it! (10% of 60 is 6, so 20% is 12).

example.problem: Find 10% of $150.

slides.title: Converting Fractions to %
slides.subtitle: Bridge the world of fractions and percentages.
slides.keyConcept: Multiply the fraction by 100% to convert to percentage: (Numerator ÷ Denominator) × 100.

example.problem: Convert 3/5 to a percentage.

slides.title: Real-Life Discounts & Markups
slides.subtitle: Master sales tags, tax, and price savings.
slides.keyConcept: Discount = Original Price × (Discount % / 100). Final Price = Original Price - Discount.
points: A $40 shirt with 25% off: 25% of 40 = $10 discount.
Final price you pay: $40 - $10 = $30.
Percentage increase: New Price = Original × (1 + % increase / 100).

example.problem: A $80 jacket is on 50% clearance. What is the sale price?

slides.title: Decimal Place Values
slides.subtitle: Understand what numbers to the right of the decimal point mean.
slides.keyConcept: First digit after point = Tenths (0.1), second = Hundredths (0.01), third = Thousandths (0.001).
points: In 3.47: 3 is Units (Wholes), 4 is 4 tenths (4/10), 7 is 7 hundredths (7/100).
Moving right from the point divides by 10 each step.
Adding zeros to the end of a decimal (like 0.5 vs 0.50) does not change its value!

example.problem: What is the place value of 6 in 4.26?
example.note: 6 is in the second spot after the decimal point, so 6 hundredths (0.06).

slides.title: The Fraction-Decimal Bridge
slides.subtitle: Effortlessly convert between fractions and decimals.
slides.keyConcept: Divide the numerator by denominator to get the decimal: 1 ÷ 2 = 0.5.

example.problem: What decimal is equal to 3/4?

slides.title: Comparing Decimals
slides.subtitle: Never be tricked by the length of a decimal number!
slides.keyConcept: Compare from left to right starting at the largest place value. Pad with trailing zeros to match lengths!
points: Common mistake: Thinking 0.19 is bigger than 0.2 because 19 > 2.
Fix: Compare 0.20 with 0.19. Since 2 tenths > 1 tenth, 0.2 > 0.19!
0.8 is much larger than 0.799.

example.problem: Which is bigger: 0.6 or 0.58?
example.note: 0.60 has 6 tenths, while 0.58 only has 5 tenths.

slides.title: Multiplying & Dividing by 10, 100
slides.subtitle: The decimal point shift superpower.
slides.keyConcept: Multiplying shifts point RIGHT. Dividing shifts point LEFT by the number of zeros!
points: Multiply by 10: Shift point 1 spot right (3.45 × 10 = 34.5).
Multiply by 100: Shift point 2 spots right (0.28 × 100 = 28).
Divide by 10: Shift point 1 spot left (45.6 ÷ 10 = 4.56).
Divide by 100: Shift point 2 spots left (72 ÷ 100 = 0.72).

example.problem: Calculate 0.09 × 100
example.note: Shift the decimal point 2 places to the right: 0.09 → 0.9 → 9.
